issues.item: Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening accident in a combat pilot, the threat profile should more plausibly center on accident recurrence, mechanical failure, bodily vulnerability, or generalized hypervigilance. 'Watching others closely for signs that they might harm me' implies an interpersonal assault/paranoia-like threat that is not supported by the trauma type or by the other selected items.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal set otherwise reflects post-traumatic identity disruption and emotional numbing ('Lost Emotions', 'Identity Loss'). 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is comparatively more characteristic of interpersonal violation or severe dissociation/depersonalization. In this profile it sits awkwardly with the accident trauma and with the other appraisal items, reducing thematic coherence of the node.

vignette: The accident occurred during a routine patrol over the Pacific when the aircraft's hydraulic system failed without warning. Tane, an American of Samoan descent, felt the violent shudder tear through the cockpit, followed by the sharp, metallic groan of control surfaces locking up. The altimeter began to spin. He fought the yoke, his muscles burning as the nose dropped and the horizon tilted. Alarms screamed in his helmet. For several minutes, the aircraft was entirely at the mercy of gravity and wind, the ground rising to meet him faster than his hands could correct. He managed to override the systems and execute a rough, shuddering landing, but the moment of suspended helplessness-the absolute loss of control while trapped in a confined metal space-left a mark that never quite faded. In the weeks that followed, Tane returned to base but found that his usual routines no longer felt safe. He had come to believe that comfort was only possible if he first identified every way out. Before he could settle into a briefing room, his eyes would dart to the rear doors, the side windows, the maintenance hatches. He mapped each exit in his mind, tracing sightlines and clearances until his shoulders finally unclenched. At home, the habit bled into his private life. He slept on the edge of the mattress, listening to the house settle, his body remaining watchful even behind locked doors and familiar walls. What frightened him most was not the silence, but the suddenness of it. He was certain that the ground could give way or the walls could breach without warning, so he stayed on guard inside his own home. Alongside this constant state of alert, Tane noticed something else shifting inside him. He would sit across from his wife at the kitchen table, watching her speak, but the conversation felt distant, muffled by a thick glass wall. He tried to recall the warmth he used to feel during their early years together, but the emotional register seemed permanently muted. He had come to believe he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. Looking in the bathroom mirror, he barely recognized the man staring back. The posture, the flat expression, the way he moved through rooms as if bracing for impact belonged to a stranger. He felt like he did not know himself anymore. The crash had taken the pilot who could trust his training; what remained was someone permanently changed for the worse. These shifts accumulated into a quiet unraveling of his daily life. He stopped attending base family gatherings because crowded rooms left him scanning every aisle, unable to bear the uncertainty of a single blocked path. When his commanding officer offered him a squadron lead position, Tane declined. The idea of sitting in a cockpit for hours, unable to map every egress, made his chest tighten. He requested a ground-assigned role instead, trading the sky for a desk where he could control his sightlines. His wife would leave plates in the sink and stop waiting up for him. The distance between them grew not from arguments, but from the sheer weight of his internal surveillance. He worked his shifts, executed his duties, and filed his reports, but the man who used to navigate storm fronts with steady hands now moved through his own home as if it were hostile territory. At fifty-four, the exhaustion of perpetual readiness finally forced him through the clinic doors. He sat across from the intake officer, palms resting on his knees, already noting the two visible exits, the placement of the fire extinguisher, the angle of the window. He had come to understand that his body was still living in the cockpit, waiting for the next mechanical failure. What he was most afraid of was that the man who had walked into the office that morning was the real one now-the one who could no longer feel, no longer trust the ground beneath him, and no longer believe he could ever return to who he had been. What he hoped for was simpler: a way to sit in a room without checking the doors, to sleep without bracing, to look at his wife and actually feel her presence again.
